title: Autonomous lawn mower
summary: Computer vision, coverage planning, and layered safety for a boundary-free autonomous lawn mower.
role: AI & perception lead · multidisciplinary capstone team
imageAlt: The team’s assembled lawn mower prototype.

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: A robot mower needs to understand both the surface it can cut and the obstacles it must avoid. Our team developed an autonomous mower concept for elderly and mobility-limited users, combining a physical platform with a modular autonomy stack.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: I led AI perception development: preparing image data, training and evaluating YOLOv8 detection and segmentation models, and connecting perception outputs with the wider robotic system. Lawn, boundary, and barrier masks support conservative cut/no-cut reasoning; object detections identify safety-relevant obstacles.

sections.title: How the system fits together
sections.text: The team combined vision with LiDAR mapping, localization, coverage planning, motion control, and safety checks. ROS nodes exchange perception and navigation information, while Gazebo and RViz support staged simulation and visualization. The project includes both ROS 1 and ROS 2 development artifacts; the documented final report describes the ROS 1 pipeline.

sections.title: Results and limits
sections.text: The recorded validation scores are 0.764 box mAP50 and 0.745 mask mAP50. The team earned an Honourable Mention at Engineering Design Day. Perception was used alongside independent safety checks; these validation scores do not measure the safety or field coverage of the complete robot.

title: Smart wheelchair navigation
summary: An indoor mobile-robot prototype exploring room navigation, hazard awareness, and arrival verification for wheelchair assistance.

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: Indoor assistive navigation needs more than a path between coordinates. The robot must recognize hazards, work around furniture, and confirm that it has reached the intended room.

sections.title: What we built
sections.text: Our team used a Yahboom Pi5 mobile robot to map a physical mock home with LiDAR and explore room-to-room navigation. OpenCV modules detected red tape representing hazardous floor zones and used color and shape cues for furniture context. QR/barcode checks provided a separate arrival signal.

sections.title: Testing and iteration
sections.text: Detector recalibration improved previously unsuccessful hazard and furniture tests. Obstacle avoidance remained partially successful, and the prototype could stall at a checkpoint if no barcode appeared. These limitations make the next steps clear: stronger recovery behavior and more robust arrival handling.

title: Gem-sorting rover — Scooper Bot 10001
summary: A constrained autonomous rover project combining pickup mechanics, color sensing, motor feedback, and sorting.
imageAlt: Full assembly CAD model explicitly labeled in the Scooper team report.

sections.title: The challenge
sections.text: The course challenge called for a rover that could collect and sort colored gems, then return to base within a time and parts budget.

sections.title: The design
sections.text: Our team used a funnel and revolving-door sorter with a color sensor inside a light-isolated chamber. ESP32-S3 firmware, encoder feedback, and motor control supported rover movement, while a servo-operated pickup mechanism handled the gems.

sections.title: Results and limitations
sections.text: The report describes pickup and color-sorting success, with return-to-base behavior limited by IR-beacon localization. This made sensing reliability and recovery an important part of the final analysis.

title: Liquid crystal elastomer soft actuators
summary: Experimental research on liquid crystal elastomers for soft robotics, from material preparation and fabrication to heat-responsive motion, load testing, and a solar-tracker demonstrator.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: During my internship at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), I worked on liquid crystal elastomers for responsive soft actuators. The project explored how a flexible polymer could produce useful motion when exposed to heat or light. The broader research direction brought together the actuator material, printed heating elements, and sensing; my experimental work focused on preparing the material, shaping it, and understanding its response.

sections.title: Fabrication and preparation
sections.text: I worked with cast LCE formulations and direct-ink-writing approaches, preparing mixtures and carrying samples through molding, stretching, and curing. I also developed sketches for laser cutting and worked with LCE elements attached to flexible silicone substrates. The fabrication work involved adjusting preparation and printing conditions, then checking whether the resulting material could be handled and tested as an actuator.

sections.title: Actuation and application tests
sections.text: I tested how the LCE strips contracted and recovered under heating and cooling, including experiments with suspended weights to see whether the material could perform mechanical work. I also tested LCE elements in a solar-tracker demonstrator, where heating one side changed the orientation of the supported solar cell. These experiments connected the behavior of the material to a possible device application.

sections.title: Thermal response and coatings
sections.text: I investigated conductive layers and light-absorbing treatments as ways to alter the thermal response. I compared coated and uncoated strips, tracked their heating and cooling behavior, and recorded changes in shape and length under heat and sunlight. The observations helped distinguish contraction, bending, and recovery, while identifying which coating and fabrication choices needed further testing.

title: Household energy forecasting
summary: Feature engineering and deep sequence models for forecasting household electricity use from smart-meter data.
role: Group project · preprocessing, features, and LSTM development

metrics.label: Reported test MAE · report target scale

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: Minute-level electricity measurements contain temporal structure, missing values, and relationships between aggregate and sub-metered consumption. A useful model needs careful data preparation as well as a suitable architecture.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: I worked on preprocessing, Power Factor and Global Active Energy features, and the LSTM architecture and tuning. The final group model used two 128-unit LSTM layers with a dense prediction head and a 256-step input window.

sections.title: Results in context
sections.text: The report records a final test R² of 0.65 and MAE of 1.07 on the project’s target scale. Earlier model attempts performed poorly, making iterative diagnosis a central part of the work. Related assignments compared ARIMA, MLP, CNN, RNN, LSTM, GRU, TCN, and Transformer-based approaches across separate datasets.

sections.title: The question

sections.title: The lab sequence
sections.text: I examined classification disparities in COMPAS data, explored fairness interventions, built causal-analysis exercises, and tested differentially private regression models. The labs connect evaluation choices with explicit assumptions about fairness and privacy.

summary: A relational database project for a multi-dealership vehicle marketplace, developed from requirements and entity modeling through SQL queries and views.

sections.title: The marketplace
sections.text: Collection of Automobile Repositories (C.A.R.) was designed as a single place to explore vehicle listings from multiple dealerships. The requirements covered searches by vehicle type, color, year, price, mileage, and dealership location, alongside comparison tools, customer accounts, and administrator inventory management.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: I helped write and develop the software description and the functionality names and descriptions in the team’s requirements specification. This work translated the marketplace idea into concrete user and administrator tasks that the database design needed to support.

sections.title: Database design
sections.text: The team modeled users, administrators, customers, dealerships, vehicles, advertisements, and reviews, then mapped those relationships to relational tables with keys and references. The schema evaluation considered how separating reviews from vehicle and customer information could reduce duplicated data and make updates easier to manage.

sections.title: SQL implementation and outputs
sections.text: The project files include table-creation scripts, sample vehicle and dealership data, a MySQL database export, update and deletion exercises, and database views. The original screenshots show a conditional vehicle-price update and a dealership-popularity view that groups dealership information with click counts. A Next.js front-end scaffold is also present; the main demonstrated deliverable here is the database and its SQL outputs.

title: Six-axis robot arm kinematics and path planning
eyebrow: Six-axis robot arm kinematics and path planning
summary: Forward and inverse kinematics, Jacobians, and potential-field path planning for a six-axis manipulator.

sections.title: The task
sections.text: We modeled a six-degree-of-freedom CrustCrawler arm for a bin-picking application, then planned end-effector motion around obstacles in the workspace.

sections.title: The implementation
sections.text: The project includes Denavit–Hartenberg forward kinematics, geometric inverse kinematics, Jacobian calculations, and potential-field planning. Parameter sweeps investigated stability and path smoothness.

sections.title: Limits and related work
sections.text: Representative planned paths avoided modeled spherical obstacles. The point-mass approximation and local minima limit what the simulation establishes. Related Baxter labs explored PID and computed-torque control on a seven-axis robot.

title: LVAD and cardiovascular modeling
role: Team biomedical systems analysis project · ECE 4455A

gallery.caption: Total modeled flow versus LVAD flow for resting and exercising conditions; the marked bends indicate where pump flow begins to dominate.
Original final-cycle arterial and ventricular pressure traces with strong LVAD support.
Original final-cycle arterial and ventricular pressure traces with the LVAD disabled.
The team’s controller-law overlay on the modeled exercise condition.

summary: A MATLAB study of how ventricular assistance changes cardiac flow, pressure, and workload, followed by a physiologically responsive LVAD control investigation.

sections.title: The question
sections.text: A left ventricular assist device supplies flow alongside a weakened heart, but stronger pump support also changes the pressures and workload of the native ventricle. Our study examined this interaction under resting and exercise conditions using a simplified cardiovascular model.

sections.title: Comparing assisted and unassisted circulation
sections.text: We varied the pump contribution and compared total systemic flow, ventricular pressure-volume loops, and ventricular and arterial pressure traces. The outputs show how increasing support can unload the ventricle until the pump supplies nearly all of the flow. Comparing the pressure traces with and without assistance helped explain when the aortic valve could open and why pulsatility changed.

sections.title: Physiologically responsive control
sections.text: We then overlaid a Starling-like supervisory control law on the relationship between pump flow and end-diastolic pressure. The aim was to select a resting operating point and examine how that same controller responded to the increased demand represented by the exercise model, while retaining a contribution from the native heart.

sections.title: Interpreting the model
sections.text: The report compares the model’s baseline filling-pressure behavior with a reference example and discusses the consequences of that mismatch. The investigation treats the outputs as simulation results: the simplified circulation, fixed parameters, and limited physiological feedback restrict how far the controller findings can be generalized.

imageAlt: Total modeled flow versus LVAD flow for resting and exercising conditions; the marked bends indicate where pump flow begins to dominate.

title: Biphasic defibrillation waveforms

gallery.caption: Original source-voltage and membrane-voltage response for a tuned-duration biphasic waveform.
Original overlay of membrane responses after fixed-tilt parameters were matched to the selected phase durations.

summary: A MATLAB investigation of how biphasic shock timing and waveform tilt change the modeled source voltage and cardiac-cell membrane response.

sections.title: Waveform timing and membrane response
sections.text: The investigation compared two ways of defining a biphasic exponential waveform: ending each phase at a specified voltage tilt, or choosing its duration directly. A cardiac-cell electrical model connected the applied source waveform with the resulting membrane-voltage response.

sections.title: What we investigated
sections.text: We examined the source time constant and energy-storage assumptions, swept the membrane time constant, and compared the membrane response at the end of each phase. The first phase was assessed for depolarization and the second for the residual membrane response after the polarity reversal.

sections.title: Matching the two parameterizations
sections.text: The final comparison converted chosen phase durations into their corresponding tilt values and ran both formulations with the same source assumptions. The resulting membrane-voltage curves nearly coincide, illustrating that matched fixed-tilt and tuned-duration settings can describe the same underlying exponential waveform.

sections.title: Project scope
sections.text: The deliverables were MATLAB calculations, waveform overlays, and a written interpretation of the electrical model. These are educational simulation results rather than device testing or clinical validation.

imageAlt: Original source-voltage and membrane-voltage response for a tuned-duration biphasic waveform.
